questions.q: What is the main signal, per this lesson, that makes a case-study portfolio read as architect-level work rather than junior-level work?
options: Showing the same decision framework applied consistently across different cases, including failure analysis and evidence of defending the design under objection -- not just presenting happy-path conclusions
Having the longest possible written descriptions for each case study
Using the most advanced vocabulary possible in every lesson
Avoiding any mention of tradeoffs or alternatives considered
questions.explain: A reviewer looks for consistency of reasoning across cases, inclusion of failure/resilience analysis, and evidence the design was stress-tested under objection -- not just polished happy-path write-ups.

questions.q: What is a 'credibility gap,' per this lesson's distinction?
options: Any gap at all in a portfolio, regardless of context
A gap that has been explicitly named as future work with a stated plan
A gap that only occurs in Chapter 1's case studies
A gap in an area the portfolio's own narrative claims to have already covered, such as calling a design 'fully resilient' without ever describing its actual resilience mechanisms
questions.explain: A credibility gap is specifically a mismatch between a claim the portfolio makes and what it actually demonstrates -- claiming full resilience while showing none of the actual mechanism undermines trust.

questions.q: Why does an honestly-named future-work gap often strengthen a portfolio rather than weaken it?
options: Because reviewers prefer portfolios with no technical content at all
Because future-work gaps are required by Salesforce certification rules
Because it demonstrates the same honest-gap-admission skill from Lesson 18 applied to the whole body of work, which is itself a signal of architect-level maturity
Because naming a gap removes the need to ever address it
questions.explain: An honestly named, not-yet-closed gap with a stated plan mirrors the honest-gap-admission pattern from Lesson 18 -- it demonstrates the same reasoning maturity at the portfolio level, rather than undermining the work.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what two reusable habits from this course should carry over into other parts of the Salesforce Architect path?
options: Memorizing every governor limit number and every Apex class name
The four-question decision framework from Lesson 8 and the comparison-matrix habit from Lesson 15
Using exactly the same company name (Doverfield) in every future course
Avoiding any discussion of failure scenarios in future courses
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly calls out the four-question framework and the comparison-matrix habit as reusable architectural judgment tools that extend well beyond integration problems specifically.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say assembling twenty individual lessons into one portfolio piece matters, beyond each lesson's standalone value?
options: Because a connected body of work demonstrating sustained, consistent reasoning across related problems is a more useful career artifact than isolated examples, and is rare enough to stand out to a reviewer
Because individual lessons have no value on their own
Because portfolios are only evaluated as a single word count total
Because assembling lessons together removes the need for Chapter 3's defense skills
questions.explain: The lesson frames the portfolio value as sustained depth across related problems -- something reviewers specifically note as uncommon and valuable, compared to one shallow example repeated multiple times.
